subject: business-studies
title: Operations Foundations Adventure
welcome_lead: You'll meet the four methods of production and learn what productivity really measures.
meta_desc: GCSE Business Studies operations foundations — job, batch, flow, mass production and productivity.
final_note: You can identify methods of production, define productivity and explain how it's measured.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Pick a method based on volume and customisation.

Job: one-off, high-skill. Batch: groups (bread loaves). Flow: continuous (cars). Mass: huge volumes (drinks cans).

Productivity = output ÷ input. Usually output per worker per hour.

If 4 workers make 200 units in an 8-hour day, productivity = 200 ÷ (4 × 8) = 6.25 units/worker/hour.

Higher productivity = lower cost per unit = bigger margins or lower prices.

It's boosted by training, motivation, better tech, lean processes, and good management.

mcqs.q: Does buying in bulk always save a business money overall?
options: Bulk-buying lowers the price per unit, but it raises storage costs, ties up cash and risks waste if demand falls — the net effect depends on the product.
Bigger orders are always cheaper for the business overall.
Bulk buying is taxed at a higher rate.
Quality is decided by the size of the advertising budget.

mcqs.q: Does higher productivity mean employees are working longer hours?
options: The only way to raise productivity is to make staff work more hours.
No — productivity is output per worker per time period; it rises through better training, equipment and methods, not necessarily longer hours.
Quality is decided by the size of the advertising budget.
Productivity measures how tidy the factory is.

mcqs.q: Is quality the same as luxury?
options: No — quality means consistently meeting customer expectations and being fit for purpose; a budget product can be high quality if it does its job reliably.
Only expensive products can be high quality.
Productivity measures how tidy the factory is.
Quality is decided by the size of the advertising budget.
